We need [latex]O(1)[/latex] MIN, without slowing down PUSH/POP. Approach: store, alongside every pushed record, a pointer to whichever record currently holds the smallest key at or below it in the stack (computed once, at push time, by comparing the new key to the previous top's "min so far" pointer). Pushing just does one comparison and one pointer copy ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); popping just removes the top record (its stored min-pointer disappears with it, automatically restoring the correct min for what's now on top) ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); MIN just reads the top record's stored pointer ([latex]O(1)[/latex]). This works and keeps everything [latex]O(1)[/latex]. A single global pointer to the current minimum fails on POP: if you pop exactly the minimum record, you have no way to find the next-smallest without scanning the rest of the stack. A sorted auxiliary array would need [latex]O(n)[/latex] shifting on push to keep it sorted. A min-heap would make push/pop cost [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] instead of [latex]O(1)[/latex], violating the "don't slow down the standard operations" requirement. Answer: Keep, with every record, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it. Click here for detail solution

Checking each claim about LL(1) parsing: - "LL(1) parser uses backtracking" — false . LL(1) is a predictive, backtrack-free top-down parser: it decides the production to use by looking at only one lookahead symbol. - "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-recursive" — false , in fact the opposite: a left-recursive grammar can never be LL(1) (it would cause infinite recursion in the predictive parser), so left recursion must first be eliminated. - "For LL(1), the grammar must be left-factored" — true . If two productions of a non-terminal share a common prefix, the parser cannot decide which one to use from one lookahead symbol; left-factoring removes this ambiguity, which is a necessary step towards making a grammar LL(1). - "LL(1) parsers are more powerful than SLR parsers" — false . LL(1) and SLR(1) are different (incomparable) classes of grammars; SLR(1), being bottom-up, actually accepts a strictly larger class of grammars than LL(1) in general, so LL(1) is not "more powerful." Answer: For a grammar to be LL(1), it must be left-factored. Click here for detail solution

When all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique , and two classical facts (cycle property and cut property) apply: - Cycle property: In any cycle [latex]C[/latex], the edge with the strictly largest weight can never appear in any MST (if it did, removing it and adding any other edge of the cycle would still keep the graph connected but reduce total weight). True. - The claim about the smallest -weight edge of every cycle being in every MST is false in general — a small edge can still be excluded if a smaller alternative path already connects its endpoints via other, even-cheaper edges from elsewhere in the graph (cycle property only rules out the *maximum*, it doesn't force in the minimum in the multi-cycle case with unrelated cycles overlapping). - The claim that the largest -weight edge touching any given vertex [latex]v[/latex] is never in any MST is false — that edge might still be the cheapest way to connect an isolated/far-off part of the graph. - Cut property: For any vertex [latex]v[/latex], consider the cut separating [latex]\{v\}[/latex] from the rest of the graph; the minimum-weight edge crossing this cut (i.e. the cheapest edge incident to [latex]v[/latex]) must belong to every MST, since choosing any costlier edge to connect [latex]v[/latex] instead would strictly increase total weight. True. Answer: The largest-weight edge in every cycle is excluded from every MST; and the smallest-weight edge incident to every vertex is included in every MST. Click here for detail solution

A memory reference passes through, in order: TLB → (page table, only if TLB misses) → cache. - TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit: possible — TLB doesn't have the mapping, page table does (page is in memory), and the corresponding cache block (whose validity depends on the page being resident) can indeed be valid and hit. Can happen. - TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible . A TLB hit means the page is currently mapped/resident in memory (TLB entries are only valid for pages currently in memory); it is therefore contradictory for the page table to then report a miss (page not in memory) for that very same page. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible . A page-table miss means the page is not in main memory at all — and the problem states that when a page is evicted, its cache blocks are marked invalid. So if the page isn't in memory, its cache blocks cannot be valid, and a cache hit is impossible. - TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss: possible and in fact the expected/consistent sequence when a page is genuinely not resident. Answer: "TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit" and "TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit" can NEVER happen. Click here for detail solution

Answer: G may contain even-length cycles; and the optimal 2-colorability test runs in Θ(|V|+|E|) time. Click here for detail solution
